lessonTitle: Developmental Delay and Cerebral Palsy: Recognition and Support

blocks.text: At his 9-month check, a boy born at 28 weeks reaches only with his left hand and keeps his right fist clenched. His mother is relieved that he is 'such a good, quiet baby' and he is smiling and babbling normally. Does this pattern suggest a global problem, an isolated one, or something with a motor cause, and who needs to be involved?

blocks.markdown: Children acquire skills in an orderly sequence across four main domains: **gross motor**, **fine motor and vision**, **speech, language and hearing**, and **social, emotional and cognitive** development. Milestones vary in timing between healthy children, so clinicians use the pattern across domains, the trajectory over time, and loss of previously acquired skills to decide whether a child needs investigation. Published age norms differ between sources; use a standard reference such as the RCPCH or Healthy Child Programme materials.

blocks.title: Global versus isolated developmental delay
blocks.text: Global developmental delay (GDD) means significant delay in two or more developmental domains in a young child. Isolated (or specific) delay affects a single domain, for example speech and language or gross motor skills, with other domains developing as expected. Loss of skills (regression) is different from delay and is always a red flag.

blocks.markdown: **Why the distinction matters.** Global delay is more often due to an underlying cause such as a genetic condition, brain malformation, perinatal brain injury, metabolic disorder or severe environmental deprivation, and predicts later learning disability. Isolated delay has a narrower differential, for example hearing loss for speech delay, or a neuromuscular or hip problem for motor delay. Evaluation includes birth and family history, growth and head circumference, dysmorphism, neurological examination, **hearing and vision tests**, and then targeted investigations chosen by a paediatrician, which commonly include genetic testing and sometimes neuroimaging and metabolic or thyroid tests, according to current local guidance.

blocks.title: Calling it global or isolated
blocks.prompt: A 30-month-old walks well, runs, stacks six cubes and plays pretend with dolls, but has only about five single words and does not follow two-step instructions. He is not responding to quiet voices. Decide how to classify the delay and plan the first steps.

steps.text: List the domains: gross motor, fine motor and play are in keeping with age; the only affected domain is speech and language (expressive and receptive).
Classify: a single domain is affected, so this is isolated speech and language delay rather than GDD.
Because suspected hearing difficulty is a treatable cause, arrange audiology promptly rather than waiting.
Plan: speech and language therapy referral, developmental review, and consider an autism assessment if social communication is also abnormal.

blocks.answer: Isolated speech and language delay with suspected hearing loss: audiology first, plus speech and language therapy.

blocks.markdown:
**Cerebral palsy (CP)** is a group of permanent, non-progressive disorders of movement and posture caused by a disturbance of the developing fetal or infant brain. The brain lesion does not progress but its clinical expression changes with growth. Causes are grouped by timing:

- **Antenatal**: cerebral malformation, congenital infection (for example cytomegalovirus), vascular events, genetic causes.
- **Perinatal**: hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, severe prematurity with intraventricular haemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia, neonatal sepsis or hypoglycaemia, severe jaundice (kernicterus).
- **Postnatal**: meningitis or encephalitis, head injury including non-accidental injury, hypoxic events.

blocks.caption: Types of cerebral palsy
rows: Increased tone, brisk reflexes, early hand preference, one side affected
Focal injury such as middle cerebral artery stroke
Increased tone in both sides; legs more than arms in diplegia
Periventricular leukomalacia of prematurity; widespread injury
Involuntary movements, dystonia or choreoathetosis, fluctuating tone
Basal ganglia injury, for example kernicterus or acute severe hypoxia

blocks.markdown: **Presentation** varies. Red flags include early hand preference before about 12 months, persistent fisting, floppy then stiff tone, abnormal posture, feeding difficulty, asymmetry and delayed motor milestones. Diagnosis is clinical and based on persistent abnormal motor patterns, supported by MRI brain in many children; CP is not diagnosed from a single abnormal neonatal sign. **Associated problems** are common and often cause more disability than the motor impairment: learning disability, epilepsy, visual and hearing impairment, speech and communication difficulty, feeding and swallowing problems with aspiration risk, drooling, gastro-oesophageal reflux, constipation, hip subluxation, scoliosis, pain, sleep disturbance and behavioural or emotional problems.

blocks.title: Working out a developmental quotient and corrected age
blocks.prompt: A girl born 10 weeks premature is now 40 weeks old (chronological age). (a) What is her corrected age in weeks? (b) A separate child aged 36 months has a developmental age of 18 months in language; compute the developmental quotient (DQ = developmental age / chronological age x 100).

steps.text: Corrected age equals chronological age minus weeks born early.
Corrected age is used when judging milestones in a premature infant, commonly up to about two years, per local practice.
Developmental quotient uses the same units for both ages.

Interpretation: a DQ of 50 shows that the language skills are at about half of expected, which is significant delay needing assessment. A DQ is a teaching tool, and formal assessments rely on standardised tests.

items: **Paediatrician**: diagnosis, coordination, epilepsy, medication, review of associated problems.
**Physiotherapist**: tone, posture, mobility, hip surveillance, orthoses and equipment.
**Occupational therapist**: hand function, daily living, seating, adaptations.
**Speech and language therapist**: communication aids, and assessment of swallowing.
**Dietitian and feeding team**: nutrition and, where needed, gastrostomy.
**Orthopaedic surgeon, ophthalmology, audiology, educational psychologist**: as needed.
**Social worker, specialist nurse, and family support**: carer assessment, equipment and short breaks.

blocks.markdown: **Education services.** In England, children with special educational needs are supported by the school's Special Educational Needs Coordinator (SENCO) and may need an **Education, Health and Care (EHC) plan** which sets out educational, health and social care needs and agreed support. Health professionals provide reports to inform needs assessment. Arrangements differ in other UK nations; check local services. The goal is for each child to participate as fully as possible, and paediatricians act as advocates alongside the family.

blocks.title: Early identification, early support
blocks.text: Do not wait for a formal diagnosis before starting therapy and support. Refer early, test hearing and vision, review associated problems regularly, and involve education from the pre-school years.

blocks.title: Regression is not delay
blocks.text: Loss of previously acquired skills, or developmental plateau with seizures, suggests a progressive neurological or metabolic disorder and needs urgent specialist evaluation. Cerebral palsy is non-progressive.

points: Global delay affects two or more domains and is more likely to have an identifiable cause and predict learning disability; isolated delay affects one domain and has a narrower differential, with hearing as a key cause of speech delay.

Cerebral palsy is a non-progressive motor disorder from developing brain injury, classified as spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic or mixed, with common associations including epilepsy, learning, vision, hearing and feeding problems.
A multidisciplinary team and education services, including SENCO and EHC planning, support the child and family.

questions.stem: Which description best defines global developmental delay?

options.text: Significant delay in two or more developmental domains
Delay only in gross motor skills with normal cognition

questions.correctOptionText: Significant delay in two or more developmental domains

distractorRationale.a: Correct: multi-domain involvement defines global delay.
distractorRationale.b: A single domain is isolated delay.
distractorRationale.c: Loss of skills is regression, a different red flag.
distractorRationale.d: A single motor domain is isolated delay.

questions.explanation: The number of affected domains separates global from isolated delay. Regression is separate and raises concern for progressive disease.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has normal walking, fine motor play and social interaction but says no words. Which first investigation is most important?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: isolated speech delay should prompt hearing testing, a treatable and common cause.
distractorRationale.b: MRI is not a first-line test for isolated speech delay.
distractorRationale.c: Muscle biopsy is for suspected myopathy.

questions.explanation: Isolated speech delay has a narrow differential, headed by hearing impairment. Early detection allows prompt treatment and language support.

questions.stem: A former preterm 3-year-old has stiff legs, a scissoring gait and relatively normal arm function. Which type of cerebral palsy is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: legs more affected than arms after prematurity matches diplegia from periventricular injury.
distractorRationale.c: Ataxic CP shows incoordination, not stiffness.

questions.explanation: Periventricular white matter injury of prematurity affects descending leg fibres closest to the ventricles, causing spastic diplegia. The scissoring gait results from adductor spasticity.

questions.stem: Which statement about cerebral palsy is correct?

options.text: The brain injury is non-progressive, though its clinical features change with growth
It is always caused by birth asphyxia
Intellectual disability is present in every child
It can be excluded by a normal MRI

questions.correctOptionText: The brain injury is non-progressive, though its clinical features change with growth

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the lesion is static but presentation evolves.
distractorRationale.b: Many causes are antenatal or postnatal; birth asphyxia accounts for a minority.
distractorRationale.c: Cognition varies from normal to severely impaired.
distractorRationale.d: A normal scan does not exclude CP, which is a clinical diagnosis.

questions.explanation: CP is defined by a non-progressive insult to the developing brain, with variable severity and cause. Diagnosis rests on clinical features and course, with imaging supportive.

questions.stem: Which professional is most directly responsible for assessing swallowing safety and communication aids in a child with cerebral palsy?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: speech and language therapists assess swallowing and communication.

questions.explanation: Speech and language therapists cover both communication and the oropharyngeal phase of swallowing. Dietitians and others contribute to feeding plans.

questions.stem: True or false: an Education, Health and Care (EHC) plan in England brings together educational, health and social care needs and support for a child with significant special educational needs.
questions.explanation: An EHC plan is a legal document that sets out the child's needs and the support to meet them across education, health and care. Health professionals contribute reports to the assessment.

questions.stem: A boy was born 8 weeks before term. He is now 52 weeks old by chronological age. What is his corrected age in weeks?
questions.explanation: Corrected age is chronological age minus the weeks born early, so 52 minus 8 is 44 weeks. Milestones in a premature infant are judged against corrected age to avoid over-diagnosing delay.

questions.stem: A child is 40 months old. On formal assessment their fine motor skills are at a 30-month level and their language skills are at a 20-month level. Using DQ = developmental age / chronological age x 100, calculate the DQ for language.
questions.explanation: Language DQ is 20 divided by 40 multiplied by 100, which is 50. The fine motor DQ would be 75, so language is the more delayed domain; delay in more than one domain would be classed as global delay.

questions.stem: Describe the common problems associated with cerebral palsy beyond movement disorder, and explain why regular review of these is part of care.
markingGuide: Feeding and swallowing problems with aspiration, reflux, drooling, poor growth
Orthopaedic problems: hip subluxation, scoliosis, contractures
Constipation, pain, sleep and behavioural or emotional problems
These often cause more disability than the motor impairment and are treatable, so regular surveillance is needed
questions.explanation: CP affects more than muscle tone, and associated problems drive quality of life and morbidity. Planned review finds problems such as hip displacement before they cause irreversible harm.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with cerebral palsy has just been offered a school place. Discuss the roles of the multidisciplinary team and the education services in supporting him.
markingGuide: Paediatrician coordinates care and manages epilepsy and associated problems
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for mobility, posture, hand function and equipment
Speech and language therapy, dietitian for communication, swallowing and nutrition
Audiology, ophthalmology, orthopaedics, psychology as needed
Education: SENCO, school support, and an EHC plan in England to specify needs and provision
Health professionals contribute reports; family at the centre; transition planning
questions.explanation: No single professional meets all needs, so team coordination around the child and family is essential. Education services turn health needs into practical support and legal entitlements at school.
